subject: Climate & Environment
title: Coastal Cities at Risk
description: A short lesson to help you apply Coastal Cities at Risk.

hook.text: Over 800 million people live in coastal cities less than 10 meters above sea level.

buildup.text: Miami, Shanghai, Mumbai, Lagos, and Jakarta all face increasing flood risk from rising seas.

discovery.text: Jakarta is sinking so fast — up to 25 cm per year — that Indonesia is building a new capital inland.

twist.text: Sea walls can buy time, but they are expensive and only work until the water overtops them.

climax.text: By 2100, trillions of dollars in coastal property could be underwater permanently.

punchline.text: The world built its biggest cities at the edge of a rising ocean.

quiz.question: Why is Indonesia building a new capital city?
options: Jakarta is sinking rapidly and flooding frequently
The government wants a more central location

details.summary: Hundreds of millions of people live in coastal zones threatened by rising seas. Cities like Jakarta, Miami, Mumbai, and Shanghai face increasing flooding, saltwater intrusion, and infrastructure damage as sea levels climb and storms intensify on warmer oceans.
details.whyItMatters: Coastal cities drive much of the global economy. Understanding their vulnerability to sea-level rise is critical for urban planning, infrastructure investment, and climate adaptation.
takeaways: Over 800 million people live in low-lying coastal areas
Storm surges on higher seas cause exponentially more damage
Saltwater intrusion threatens freshwater supplies in many cities

faq.question: Which major cities are most at risk from sea-level rise?
faq.answer: Jakarta, Miami, Mumbai, Shanghai, Lagos, and Bangkok are among the most vulnerable due to low elevation, large populations, and subsidence. Jakarta is sinking so fast from groundwater extraction that Indonesia is relocating its capital.

faq.question: How do cities adapt to rising seas?
faq.answer: Strategies include building seawalls and flood barriers, restoring mangroves and wetlands for natural protection, elevating infrastructure, improving drainage systems, and in extreme cases relocating communities to higher ground.
